title: Prayer for the Fallen
sum: The treaties of chapter 11 do not stop the local commanders. The people of Joppa drown two hundred Jews in a staged boat trip, and Judas burns their harbor, and Jamnia's too. He then marches east of the Jordan: he beats a band of nomads and makes peace with them, storms Caspin, routs Timothy's huge army, takes Carnion and its shrine of Atargatis and the walled town of Ephron, but spares Scythopolis, whose Jews speak for their neighbors. After the Feast of Weeks he fights Gorgias in Idumea; a few Jews fall, and Gorgias escapes.

After the Sabbath, Judas's men go to bring the fallen home and find, under every dead man's tunic, charms of the idols of Jamnia. They bless God, who brought the hidden thing to light, and pray that the sin be wiped away. Judas collects two thousand drachmas and sends them to Jerusalem for a sin offering. The writer explains: Judas did it because he believed in the resurrection, and it was a holy and godly thought; "That is why he had atonement made for the dead, to free them from the sin" (12:45).
readings: Most of the chapter is a record of raids and sieges in the coastal plain and in Gilead, close to 1 Maccabees 5 but told with bigger numbers and more prayers. The writer shows Judas punishing cities that attacked Jews and sparing one that treated them well.
Read as a lesson about sin and the dead

The last eight verses turn a battle report into a lesson: hidden sin brings death, God reveals it, the living pray for the guilty dead, and the hope of resurrection makes that prayer sensible. For Catholic and Orthodox readers this is the clearest Old Testament witness to prayer for the dead; Protestant readers take the moral warning and set the doctrine aside.

views.C: The Catholic Church reads 12:38–45 as Scripture teaching that the living can help the dead by prayer and sacrifice. The Catechism cites it for the practice of praying for the dead and for the purification of the elect after death (1032), and the Roman Lectionary offers 12:43–46 (12:43–45 here) among the readings for Masses for the dead. Catholic interpreters note that the men died fighting for the law, so they were not lost, yet they carried a sin: the case purgatory describes.
views.O: Orthodox churches cite the passage for their constant prayer for the departed, above all at the Divine Liturgy and on the Saturdays of the Dead. They do not draw from it the Latin teaching of a cleansing fire. Mark of Ephesus argued at the council of Ferrara-Florence (at Ferrara, 1438) that the passage shows prayers and offerings helping the dead, but says nothing of fire or of punishment that satisfies justice.
views.P: Protestant churches do not use the passage to establish doctrine, since they do not count the book as canonical. Calvin granted that Judas acted from hope in the resurrection, but said the offering was not free of superstition, and that the writer's own judgment carries no authority. Many Protestant readers value the chapter's warning that hidden sin is found out (12:40–42).
views.H: Historians think the story keeps a real event: the dead were found with amulets from Jamnia, and Judas sent money for a sin offering. Many think the offering was meant to purify the living army of guilt, as with Achan, and that the writer, a believer in resurrection, read it as help for the dead. The text is also an early witness to the idea that the dead's state can change after death.
views.J: Rabbinic Judaism did not keep 2 Maccabees and never cites this passage, but it developed its own ways of helping the dead: charity and remembrance on Yom Kippur (later Yizkor), and the mourner's Kaddish, said for eleven months. Sifre on Deuteronomy reads Deuteronomy 21:8 as teaching that the dead need atonement.

deep.h: What Judas did, and what the writer made of it
deep.b:
The story has two layers. In the first, Judas's men find idol charms on the dead, conclude that this was why they died, bless God's justice, and pray that "the sin that had been done be wiped away entirely" (12:42). Judas takes up a collection and sends it to Jerusalem for a sin offering. Read alone, this could be an act to cleanse the camp, as Israel had to remove Achan's sin before it could stand against its enemies (Joshua 7:12–13).

In the second layer, the writer comments (12:43b–45). He says Judas acted "very fine and gracious" because he had the resurrection in mind; without that hope it would be pointless and silly "to pray for the dead"; and so "he had atonement made for the dead, to free them from the sin", the sin of 12:40–42. The writer, then, understands the offering as being for the dead men themselves. It is one of the oldest clear statements in Jewish literature that the living can do something to free the dead from sin (compare Tobit 4:17 and Baruch 3:4, whose dates and sense are debated).

deep.h: Prayer for the dead in the early church
deep.b:
Christians prayed for their dead from early times. Tertullian, about AD 200, speaks of offerings for the dead on the anniversary of their death; the North African martyr Perpetua prays in prison for her dead brother Dinocrates and sees him relieved; Christian tomb inscriptions ask the reader to pray for the person buried there. Cyril of Jerusalem, about AD 350, explains that the Eucharist is offered for those who have fallen asleep (Catechetical Lectures 23.9–10). Augustine, in On the Care to Be Had for the Dead, cites this chapter, though he adds that the church's custom would be enough without it.

The Latin West later framed this practice in the doctrine of purgatory, first set out in the profession of faith of the Second Council of Lyons (1274) and defined at Florence (1439) and Trent (1563). The Reformers rejected purgatory and, with it, the prayers and Masses offered for the dead. The Orthodox kept the prayers and rejected the Latin definition. The passage stands at the center of all three positions.

echoes: Joshua 6:20; Joshua 7:1–26; Deuteronomy 7:25–26; Numbers 31:19–24; Genesis 49:29; 2 Samuel 21:14; Psalm 51:1; Leviticus 4:1–35; Deuteronomy 21:8; Daniel 12:2; 1 Corinthians 15:29; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14

settings.by: the citizens of Joppa, by a common decree of the city
settings.when: about 163 BC, after the treaties of chapter 11
settings.why: To lure the Jews onto boats as if for a friendly outing, and then drown them.
settings.readers: For readers in Egypt, who lived as a minority in Greek cities, the story warned how quickly civic friendship could turn; the writer stresses that the Jews agreed because they wanted to live in peace (12:4). Scholars debate whether the decree was a real civic act or the writer's dramatization.

settings.when: during the campaign east of the Jordan, 163 BC
settings.why: To end the fighting by offering livestock and service in exchange for peace.
settings.readers: The book's first readers were Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt, to whom the opening letters are addressed (1:1, 10); nothing in this passage points to a narrower audience. Jews living among Gentiles in Egypt would read a pact honestly kept with non-Jews as a model for their own dealings.

settings.when: before the assault on Caspin
settings.why: To ask for victory over a city that trusted its walls and blasphemed, recalling the fall of Jericho.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10), who knew Joshua in Greek: the grandson of Ben Sira, in Egypt after 132 BC, already speaks of the Law and the Prophets in translation. They would recognize the Jericho story the prayer recalls.

settings.when: after the rout at Carnion
settings.why: To save his life by threatening the Jewish captives he held, the parents and brothers of Judas's men.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10). The writer assumes they know Timothy from earlier chapters (8:30–33; 10:24–37), where his death has already been told, so the order of the episodes would puzzle a careful first reader as it puzzles scholars now.

settings.to: the Sovereign "who crushes the strength of enemies with his might"
settings.when: before the assault on Ephron
settings.why: To ask God's help against a fortified town with strong defenders and many siege engines.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10). The prayer's title for God, "Sovereign", is the one the book uses throughout (3:24; 15:29), so its first readers would hear the same God addressed in every battle.

settings.what: The Jews of Scythopolis speak for their city
settings.when: on the march back toward Jerusalem
settings.why: To testify that the Gentiles of Scythopolis had treated them kindly, and so to spare the city.
settings.readers: The scene answers the Joppa story: Greek cities that treat Jews well are treated well. For readers in Alexandria it modeled good relations with Gentile neighbors. 1 Maccabees 5:52 does not mention it.

settings.when: in the battle against Gorgias, when Esdris's men were exhausted
settings.why: To ask the Lord to appear as ally and leader, and to lead the war cry with hymns in the ancestral language.
settings.readers: The "ancestral language" (Hebrew or Aramaic) set off the moment for Greek-speaking readers; the writer uses the same phrase for the martyrs (7:8, 21, 27). Whether hymns before battle followed a set form, like the priests' trumpets of Numbers 10:9, is unknown.

settings.what: The army's prayer and Judas's sin offering, with the writer's comment
settings.by: the army and Judas; then the writer, in his own voice
settings.when: the day after the Sabbath at Adullam, 163 BC
settings.why: To ask that the sin of the dead be wiped away, to warn the living, and to send an offering to Jerusalem; then, in the writer's comment, to explain the act by the hope of resurrection.
settings.readers: Early readers who already believed in resurrection, like the writer, would find the act natural; others, perhaps Sadducees, would not. Scholars debate whether Judas meant to purify the living camp, and whether the comment in 12:43b–45 is the writer's addition or comes from Jason of Cyrene. Since the Reformation the passage has been the chief proof text in the dispute over purgatory.

traditions.q: Judas had atonement made for the dead, "to free them from the sin" (12:45). Can sins be cleansed after death, as the Catholic teaching on purgatory holds? (For the wider question whether the living may pray for the departed, see the card at Psalm 130.)
views: Yes. Those who die in God's grace but not yet fully purified undergo a purification after death, so as to reach the holiness needed for heaven, and the living help them by prayer, works of penance and above all the Eucharist. The Council of Florence (1439) and the Council of Trent (session 25, 1563) defined that purgatory exists and that the souls there are helped by the suffrages of the faithful. The Catechism cites this passage: Judas "made atonement for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin" (1032). The Catechism joins the passage to the Lord's word about sins not forgiven "in the age that is coming" (Matthew 12:32), to Paul's image of being saved as through fire (1 Corinthians 3:15), and to the church's prayer for the dead from its earliest days (1031–1032). Trent counted 2 Maccabees among the sacred books (session 4).

The departed are helped by the prayers of the church, by the Liturgy and by almsgiving, and the Orthodox pray for them in every service. But there is no purgatorial fire and no temporal punishment that pays off a debt to God's justice. At the council of Ferrara-Florence (at Ferrara, 1438), Mark of Ephesus argued that the prayers and offerings of 2 Maccabees 12 help the dead, and that the passage is "less a proof of the existence of purgatorial fire than a refutation of it", since it speaks of forgiveness, not of fire.

No. Christ's satisfaction frees the believer from sin and its penalty, so nothing remains to be purged after death. The Smalcald Articles (II.2.12–15) reject purgatory, with the Masses, vigils and works for souls there, as a human invention resting on the Mass for the dead, which cannot be established from Scripture. The Apology of the Augsburg Confession (XXIV) attacks the applying of the Mass to the dead to win them release, but says plainly that it does not forbid prayer for the dead. Luther's own handling of this passage at Leipzig (1519) is told on the book page.

No. Calvin granted that Judas acted from hope in the resurrection but said his offering was not free of superstition and misguided zeal, and that the book, whose writer asks pardon for his style, is no oracle of the Holy Spirit (Institutes 3.5.8). The Westminster Confession teaches that at death the souls of the righteous are made perfect in holiness and received into heaven, and that Scripture knows no place for souls after death besides heaven and hell (32.1). (Its rule against prayer for the dead, 21.4, is on the Psalm 130 card.)

The Thirty-Nine Articles call "the Romish Doctrine concerning Purgatory" a thing "vainly invented, and grounded upon no warranty of Scripture" (Article XXII), and say the church reads books such as 2 Maccabees "for example of life" but does not use them "to establish any doctrine" (Article VI).

title: The Boy King's Invasion
sum: In the year 149 (163 BC) the boy king Antiochus V and his regent Lysias march on Judea with a huge army, elephants and scythed chariots. Menelaus, the high priest who had served the persecutors, joins them, hoping to keep his office. But God turns the king against him: Lysias blames him for all the trouble, and he is taken to Beroea and dropped into a tower of ashes. He sinned at the altar, whose fire and ash were holy, and died in ash.

Judas calls the people to three days of weeping and fasting, takes counsel with the elders, and attacks the royal camp near Modein by night with the password "God's victory", killing many and the leading elephant. The king tries Beth-zur, fails again and again, and a Jewish traitor is caught. Hearing that Philip has rebelled in Antioch, the king makes peace on fair terms, sacrifices and honors the temple, and leaves Hegemonides as governor. Lysias calms the angry people of Ptolemais and returns to Antioch.
readings: 1 Maccabees tells the same campaign with a defeat: Judas withdraws after the battle of Beth-zechariah, his brother Eleazar dies under an elephant, Beth-zur surrenders in a Sabbath year, and the king breaks his oath and tears down the temple wall (1 Maccabees 6:28–63). 2 Maccabees leaves all this out and tells only of victories and an honorable peace.

The chapter is built on the book's idea of fitting punishment. Menelaus, who defiled the altar, dies in ash; the king who came to do the worst ends by honoring the temple. Prayer and fasting come before the victory, and the king of kings stands over the boy king.

views.O: The Orthodox Church keeps the Maccabean martyrs as saints on August 1, but this chapter, with its battles and its execution of Menelaus, is not read in the services. Orthodox readers take it as history within the book the church receives.
views.P: Protestant historians have often trusted 1 Maccabees 6 over this chapter where the two differ, judging that 2 Maccabees leaves out Judas's defeat at Beth-zechariah and the king's broken oath (1 Maccabees 6:47, 62).
views.H: Historians place the campaign in 163/162 BC and generally follow 1 Maccabees on its course. 2 Maccabees adds the execution of Menelaus at Beroea, which 1 Maccabees does not mention and Josephus confirms. Both books agree that Philip's rebellion forced the sudden peace (1 Maccabees 6:55–63).
views.J: Rabbinic literature does not name Menelaus; his end is known from this chapter and from Josephus, who adds that Alcimus succeeded him. The three days of weeping and fasting before the battle match the public fasts in time of danger that the Mishnah later regulates (tractate Taanit).

deep.b:
1 Maccabees 6 gives the campaign of Antiochus V in detail: the siege of the Citadel by Judas, the king's march with 100,000 foot, 20,000 horse and 32 elephants, the battle of Beth-zechariah where Eleazar killed an elephant and died, Judas's retreat, the surrender of Beth-zur for lack of food in a Sabbath year, the siege of the temple mount, and the sudden peace when Philip came back to Antioch, followed by the king's breaking of his oath (1 Maccabees 6:18–63).

2 Maccabees 13 keeps the outline (the boy king, Lysias, the elephants, Beth-zur, Philip, the peace) but changes its color. The night raid near Modein is a victory, Beth-zur holds out, and the king makes a generous peace and honors the temple. Each book shapes the story to its aims. 1 Maccabees is open about defeats because it praises the family's endurance; 2 Maccabees shows God defending the temple and its faithful people.

Menelaus held the high priesthood from about 172 to 163 BC. He bought it from Antiochus IV (4:24), had Onias murdered (4:34), robbed the temple vessels (4:32, 39) and guided the king into the sanctuary (5:15). Josephus confirms his execution and adds that Lysias advised it, that it took place at Beroea, and that Alcimus succeeded him (Antiquities 12.384–385).

The execution was politics: the new government had ended the persecution (11:22–26) and needed someone to blame for it. The writer sees it as justice. He describes the strange tower of ash in detail, then closes with the moral: "in ash he received his death" (13:8).

echoes: Ezra 7:12; Daniel 2:37; Leviticus 6:10–13; Esther 4:16; Judges 7:19–22; Jeremiah 22:19

settings.by: King Antiochus V, on Lysias's advice
settings.when: 163 BC, on the march to Judea
settings.why: To have Menelaus taken to Beroea and executed there.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10), who had read in chapters 4–5 of this same book how Menelaus bought the high priesthood and had Onias killed. Some may also have known Jason of Cyrene's five books, which the writer summarizes (2:23).

settings.what: Judas's call to prayer and the people's plea
settings.by: Judas, and then the whole people
settings.to: the people, and the merciful Lord
settings.when: as the royal army approached, 163 BC
settings.why: To bring the nation to three days of weeping, fasting and prayer that God would not let them lose the law, the homeland and the temple.
settings.readers: The three-day fast echoes Esther 4:16, and the list "the law, ... their homeland and ... the holy temple" names what the book is about. Readers in Egypt, who kept Hanukkah by the letter of 1:9, were reminded what the feast had saved.

settings.when: near Modein, before the night attack
settings.why: To commit the outcome to God and urge them to fight to the death for the laws, the temple, the city, the homeland and their way of life.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10), for whom "the laws, the temple, the city, the homeland" were mostly far away; the opening letters urge them to share in Jerusalem's feasts (1:9, 18). Watchwords were familiar to anyone who knew Greek armies, in which Jews in Egypt served.

settings.to: the Jews, and the defenders of Beth-zur
settings.when: 163 BC, after news of Philip's revolt
settings.why: To make peace in haste, swear to fair terms, and honor the temple, so as to return to Antioch.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10), who lived under Ptolemaic kings and would value a story of a Gentile king honoring the temple. Readers who also knew 1 Maccabees 6:62 would meet a different memory of the same peace.

settings.what: Lysias's defense before the people of Ptolemais
settings.when: 163 BC, on the way back to Antioch
settings.why: To defend the treaty with the Jews and calm a hostile Greek city.
settings.readers: The scene assumes readers familiar with Greek civic assemblies. Its quick verbs make Lysias's skill the point; whether a regent would really argue before a city in this way is debated.

title: Alcimus, Nicanor and Razis
sum: Three years later Demetrius I lands at Tripolis and takes the throne. Alcimus, a former high priest who had defiled himself in the persecution, goes to him with a golden crown and accuses Judas and the Hasideans of keeping the war alive. Demetrius sends Nicanor as governor to kill Judas and install Alcimus. But Nicanor, wary of Judas's men, makes a treaty, meets Judas in person and grows fond of him, and urges him to marry and settle down. Alcimus reports the friendship to the king, who orders Judas sent to Antioch in chains. Judas sees the change in Nicanor and goes into hiding.

Nicanor comes to the temple and demands Judas. When the priests swear they do not know where he is, Nicanor stretches out his hand toward the sanctuary and swears to level it and build a temple to Dionysus. The priests pray to the Lord who needs nothing but chose to dwell among them. Then Nicanor sends five hundred soldiers to seize Razis, an elder called "father of the Jews". Trapped, Razis falls on his sword, throws himself from the wall, runs through the crowd, and on a rock tears out his bowels and flings them at his enemies, calling on the Lord of life to give them back to him.
readings: The chapter covers 162–161 BC: Demetrius's arrival, Alcimus's appointment, Nicanor's mission. Its account of a real friendship between Nicanor and Judas differs from 1 Maccabees 7, which calls Nicanor treacherous from the start, and many historians think 2 Maccabees is closer to the facts here.

Razis's death is the book's last martyr story. Like Eleazar and the seven brothers, he chooses death over surrender and dies hoping for the resurrection of the body. But unlike them he takes his own life, and that difference has divided readers since Augustine.

views.C: Catholic teaching follows Augustine: the book narrates Razis's death without making it a model, and the commandment against killing applies to oneself. Catholic commentators praise his loyalty and his hope of the resurrection, while denying that suicide can be right.
views.O: Orthodox readers honor Razis's zeal but, with the fathers, do not hold up his manner of death as an example; the church's canons forbid suicide (canon 14 of Timothy of Alexandria, received by the Orthodox, denies the offering and prayers of the church to one who kills himself while in his right mind). The priests' prayer, which praises the God who needs nothing yet dwells among his people, is read as a type of God's presence in the church.
views.P: Protestant critics of the book's canonicity, from the Reformation on, pointed to the praise of Razis's suicide as a sign that the book is not inspired. Protestant historians have also valued the chapter's picture of Nicanor's friendship with Judas as evidence for the course of events in 162–161 BC.
views.H: Historians accept the outline: Demetrius I took the throne in 162 BC, Alcimus was made high priest, and Nicanor was sent as governor. They debate the friendship of Nicanor and Judas, and many find 2 Maccabees more credible than 1 Maccabees on it. Razis is unknown elsewhere; his story is shaped by Greek ideals of the noble death.
views.J: Jewish law forbids suicide, though rabbinic tradition honored those who died rather than be forced into sin, such as the four hundred captives who threw themselves into the sea (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 57b). Some scholars identify Alcimus with Yakim of Tseroroth, who in a midrash mocks his uncle, the sage Yose ben Yoezer, on the way to execution, and then repents and takes his own life (Genesis Rabbah 65:22).

deep.b:
1 Maccabees tells the story in a few lines: Nicanor sent "a treacherous message of peace", met Judas, but "the enemy were ready to seize Judas" (1 Maccabees 7:27–29). 2 Maccabees has a fuller story: a treaty approved by the troops, private meetings with guards posted, a real friendship, Judas's marriage, and then a royal order that forced Nicanor to turn (14:18–30). Many historians think the longer story is the better one: it explains why Nicanor did not simply attack, and why the king needed to intervene.

The writer of 2 Maccabees has his own reason to tell it: once Nicanor is shown to be a decent man, his oath against the temple (14:33) is a free choice, and his end is the more deserved. 1 Maccabees, which wants Nicanor evil from the start, has no need for the friendship.

The writer leaves no doubt about his own view. Razis was "devoted to his people", had risked body and soul for Judaism, and died "nobly" and "like a true man" (14:37–43). His last act is a prayer for resurrection (14:46). The writer sets him in the line of Eleazar and the seven brothers.

Christian readers were troubled. When Donatists in North Africa praised members who killed themselves, citing Razis, Augustine answered that Scripture reports many deeds it does not approve, and that Razis, though great, "was not wise in choosing death" but "impatient in bearing humiliation" (Letter 204). Aquinas followed him (Summa II-II 64.5). Jewish law, too, forbids suicide, while honoring those who died to avoid being forced to sin. The story is a test case for how a sacred book's narrator and its readers' moral judgment relate.

echoes: Deuteronomy 32:9; Joshua 7:6; Nehemiah 9:1; 1 Kings 8:27; Psalm 50:12; Acts 17:25; Exodus 25:8; John 1:14; Judges 16:30; 1 Samuel 31:4; Galatians 1:13–14

settings.to: King Demetrius I and his council
settings.when: 162 BC, soon after Demetrius took the throne
settings.why: To win back the high priesthood by painting Judas and the Hasideans as rebels who keep the kingdom from peace.
settings.readers: The speech is a hostile witness: the writer lets Judas's enemy describe him as the Hasideans' leader. Readers comparing 1 Maccabees 7:12–16, where Alcimus kills sixty Hasideans who trusted him, would see the same treachery. Scholars use the speech in the debate over who the Hasideans were.

settings.when: 162 BC
settings.why: To have Nicanor kill Judas, scatter his men and make Alcimus high priest.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10). The writer gives the substance of the royal letters, as Jason of Cyrene may have done (2:23); readers had no copy, unlike the letters quoted in full in chapter 11.

settings.what: The people's prayer at Nicanor's approach
settings.to: God, who set up his people for all time
settings.when: as Nicanor's army and the Gentiles of Judea advanced, 162 BC
settings.why: To ask God, with dust on their heads, to help his own portion as he always had, with an appearance.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10), who read the Torah in Greek and would know "his own portion" from Deuteronomy 32:9. The opening letters ask them to pray for Jerusalem (1:6), as the people pray here.

settings.what: Alcimus's accusation and the king's letter
settings.when: 161 BC
settings.why: To break the friendship of Nicanor and Judas: Alcimus charges disloyalty, and the king orders Judas sent to Antioch in chains.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10), many of whom lived near royal courts and knew how a rival's report could change a king's mind. The writer's word for Alcimus, "thoroughly evil", tells them how to judge him.

settings.when: 161 BC, after Judas went into hiding
settings.why: To force the priests to surrender Judas by threatening to level the temple and build one to Dionysus.
settings.readers: 1 Maccabees 7:35 gives a shorter oath, to burn the temple. Both books use it to make Nicanor's death a judgment. For readers in Egypt, Dionysus was the god of the Ptolemies' festivals, and the threat would sound concrete.

settings.when: 161 BC, after Nicanor's oath
settings.why: To ask God, who needs nothing but chose to dwell among them, to keep the newly cleansed temple undefiled forever.
settings.readers: The prayer recalls the rededication of Hanukkah ("newly cleansed"), the feast the book's opening letters urge Egyptian Jews to keep (1:9, 18). It is answered in 15:34, almost word for word.

settings.to: "the one who rules over life and spirit"
settings.when: 161 BC, at the moment of his death
settings.why: To ask God to give back the body he was losing.
settings.readers: The prayer is the book's clearest statement of bodily resurrection after 7:11. Early Christian readers used it for the resurrection of the flesh; others noted that a prayer does not make the manner of death right.

title: Nicanor's Day
sum: Nicanor plans to attack Judas's men in Samaria on the Sabbath. When the Jews in his army object, he mocks: is there a Sovereign in heaven who ordered the Sabbath? He is a sovereign on earth. But his plan comes to nothing. Judas encourages his men from the Law and the Prophets and tells them a dream: the murdered high priest Onias, praying for the whole people, and then Jeremiah, in glory, "the one who prays much for the people and the holy city", who gives Judas a golden sword from God.

Before the battle Judas prays to the God who sent his angel against Sennacherib. The Jews fight with their hands and pray with their hearts, and Nicanor falls. They cut off his head and the hand he had raised against the temple, display them in Jerusalem, feed his tongue to the birds, and bless the Lord who kept his place undefiled. All vote to keep the thirteenth of Adar every year, "one day before Mordecai's Day". The writer ends: if the work is well done, that is what he wanted; if it is modest, it was what he could do; and like wine mixed with water, a well-made story pleases its readers.
readings: Read as the founding of a feast
The book's main story ends with a festival, as its middle had (10:1–8). Nicanor's Day on 13 Adar sits beside Purim on 14 Adar; both celebrate the defeat of an enemy who meant to destroy the Jews.
Read as the communion of saints

Judas's dream shows the faithful dead alive and praying for Israel: Onias the murdered priest and Jeremiah the prophet. For Catholic and Orthodox readers it is the classic Old Testament text for the intercession of the saints; Protestant readers take it as a dream, valued for its comfort, not as doctrine.

views.C: Catholic theologians cite 15:12–14 for the intercession of the saints: those who are with God pray for the living, and Jeremiah is called the one "who prays much for the people". Catholic writers also answer the Protestant use of 15:38 by noting that inspiration does not take away a human author's style or effort.
views.O: Orthodox readers see in Onias and Jeremiah the saints who stand before God for the world, and they invoke the saints in every service. The church keeps the Maccabees and Eleazar as saints of the old covenant, and Jeremiah's role as intercessor fits the Orthodox hymns that ask the prophets' prayers.
views.P: Protestant confessions do not invoke the saints, though some, like the Lutheran Apology, grant that the saints pray for the church in general. They read Judas's dream as a dream, not as revelation. Calvin and many after him cited the writer's apology in 15:38 as proof that the book is not inspired.
views.H: Historians date Nicanor's defeat to 13 Adar 161 BC, confirmed by 1 Maccabees 7:43–49, Josephus and the Scroll of Fasts. 15:36 is the earliest witness to Purim outside Esther. The ending before Judas's death, a year later, is a literary choice; the claim that the Hebrews held the city from then on (15:37) is not true of the following years.
views.J: The Scroll of Fasts lists "the day of Nicanor" on 13 Adar as a day on which fasting is forbidden, and the Talmud tells the story of Nicanor's defeat (Ta'anit 18b). Josephus says it was still kept in his day (Antiquities 12.412); it lapsed when the rabbis set aside the Scroll of Fasts (Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 18b). 13 Adar is now the Fast of Esther, first attested in geonic times.

deep.h: Onias and Jeremiah: the dead who pray
deep.b:
The dream has two figures. Onias III, whom the book introduced as the godly high priest of a peaceful city (3:1) and whose murder it told (4:34), stands with hands outstretched in the posture of prayer, interceding for all the Jews. Then Jeremiah appears, glorious and white-haired, and Onias introduces him as "the lover of his brothers, the one who prays much for the people and the holy city" (15:14). Jeremiah gives Judas a golden sword.

The scene assumes that the righteous dead are alive with God and care for Israel. Later Jewish texts tell of the patriarchs and of Moses pleading for Israel, and Baruch asks God to hear "the prayer of the dead of Israel" (Baruch 3:4). Christians read the scene in the light of Revelation's prayers of the saints (Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4). Whether the living may ask such prayers is where the churches part ways; the question is carded at Revelation 5.

2 Maccabees and 1 Maccabees agree that the people decreed a yearly feast on 13 Adar (1 Maccabees 7:49; 15:36). The Scroll of Fasts, an Aramaic list of joyful days from the first century AD, includes it, and the Talmud remembers the story (Ta'anit 18b). Josephus says the Jews kept it every year in his day (Antiquities 12.412).

Placing it "one day before Mordecai's Day" ties the two feasts: in Esther the Jews fought their enemies on 13 Adar and rested on the 14th (Esther 9:17). A Greek-speaking reader, who may have known Esther in its Greek form, would see Judas's victory as a second Purim. The feast later lapsed with the rest of the Scroll of Fasts, and 13 Adar is now the Fast of Esther, first attested in geonic times.

Greek historians often closed with a word about their style, and this writer had opened with a long preface on the labor of making a summary (2:24–32). He ends in the same voice: he hoped to write well; if the result is modest, that was what he could reach; and a story, like wine mixed with water, should give pleasure as well as facts (15:38–39).

Protestant writers, from Calvin on, argued that an author who speaks so is not writing under the Holy Spirit's direction. Catholic and Orthodox writers reply that human effort and modesty do not exclude inspiration, as Luke's careful research does not (Luke 1:1–4). The question belongs to the whole book; see the card on the book page. See also the variant on 15:38: the Latin, unlike the Greek, has the writer ask pardon.

echoes: Exodus 5:2; Matthew 7:12; Jeremiah 15:1; Matthew 16:14; Revelation 5:8; 1 Samuel 17:47; 2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36; Exodus 23:20; Exodus 17:11–12; 1 Samuel 17:54; Esther 9:1; Esther 9:17–22; Isaiah 1:22; Luke 1:1–4

settings.by: the Jews forced to march with Nicanor; Nicanor
settings.when: 161 BC, as Nicanor planned a Sabbath attack in Samaria
settings.why: The Jews ask him to honor the day God made holy; Nicanor mocks the idea of a Sovereign in heaven and claims to be sovereign on earth.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10), who served in Gentile armies and courts and knew the strain between royal orders and the Sabbath. Readers of Exodus in Greek would hear Pharaoh's challenge (Exodus 5:2) in Nicanor's.

settings.when: 161 BC, before the battle
settings.why: To give them courage from the Law and the Prophets, past victories, the enemy's oath-breaking and a dream worth believing.
settings.readers: The mention of "the Law and the Prophets" (15:9) is valuable evidence for how the writer's community named its scriptures. The speech is reported, not quoted; scholars see the writer's style throughout.

settings.by: Onias and Jeremiah, in Judas's dream; Judas reports it
settings.to: Judas, and through him the army
settings.when: 161 BC, the night before the battle
settings.why: Onias introduces Jeremiah as the people's great intercessor, and Jeremiah gives Judas a golden sword from God for the victory.
settings.readers: For the first readers, Onias was a recent martyr (4:34) and Jeremiah the prophet linked with the temple's treasures (2:1–8). Since the Reformation the scene has been a main text in the debate over the intercession of the saints.

settings.to: the Lord, the Master and Sovereign of the heavens
settings.when: 161 BC, facing Nicanor's army with its elephants
settings.why: To ask God, who sent his angel against Sennacherib, to send a good angel ahead of them and strike terror into the blasphemers.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10). The prayer recalls Sennacherib, as Judas's earlier prayer did (8:19); readers of 1 Maccabees would find the same memory at 1 Maccabees 7:41–42, which suggests a shared Jerusalem tradition.

settings.when: 161 BC, on finding Nicanor dead
settings.why: To bless God in the ancestral language for the victory.
settings.readers: Greek-speaking Jews, probably in Egypt (1:1, 10), for whom Greek was the daily language. The writer marks that the victory blessing was in their fathers' tongue, as were the martyrs' words (7:8, 21, 27).

settings.what: The blessing of the Lord who appears
settings.when: 161 BC, in Jerusalem
settings.why: To bless God who kept his place free from defilement.
settings.readers: The blessing answers the priests' prayer of 14:36. For readers in Egypt urged to keep the temple's feasts (1:9, 18), it sealed the story with the temple safe.

settings.by: the whole people, by common vote
settings.to: all Jews, in every year to come
settings.when: 161 BC
settings.why: To make 13 Adar, the day before Mordecai's Day, a yearly feast.
settings.readers: 1 Maccabees 7:49 records the same decree, Josephus says it was kept in his day, and the Scroll of Fasts lists it. Its link with Purim suggests that readers already knew Mordecai's Day.

settings.when: after 124 BC (the date of the first opening letter, 1:9), between about 124 BC and the 60s BC
settings.why: To close his summary with a word on its style and purpose: to please as well as to inform.
settings.readers: Greek readers expected such a closing. Since Calvin it has been cited in the debate over inspiration; Catholic and Orthodox writers answer that the human author's effort does not rule out inspiration.
